(CNN) — A visit backstage at Cirque du Soleil can be brutal for your confidence. Anthony Gatto says he began practicing at age 3 and started performing when he was 8.

Inside the performers’ tent for the touring production “Kooza,” muscular men launch their partners from an enormous seesaw onto one another’s shoulders, while a female performer twists her body into extraordinary positions atop child-size blocks. After watching enough of this, you may find yourself searching for someone more ordinary to restore your ego.

That person might appear to be the man off to the side in a T-shirt, shorts and sneakers, casually tossing balls into the air. Surely that cannot be too difficult.

Any remaining confidence disappears when he balances and bounces a soccer ball on his head while simultaneously jumping rope. Soon afterward, he is juggling six or seven orange rings so quickly that they become a blur. With every ring still airborne, he spins in a pirouette and then catches them all on his arm. Watch the juggler perform »

In a sense, Gatto followed in his family’s professional footsteps—except his stepfather was neither a physician nor a farmer. He was a juggler.

“When I was 8, I entered a juggling contest, and Patrick Dempsey, who is now an actor, happened to compete in the same event,” Gatto said. “He used to juggle. I came in first and he finished second. Today he’s a major actor, while I’m still here juggling.”

That description understates Gatto’s success. He never had to try out for “Kooza”; the production actively sought him out.

“I currently hold 11 world records in juggling,” he said. “I’ve had some of them since I was 16, and no one has broken them yet.”

Gatto’s tight stage costume resembles a disco ball that can be worn. Behind the scenes, however, he dresses in a long-sleeved T-shirt, athletic shorts and sneakers. His clothing may be relaxed, but his schedule is anything but. He usually trains and rehearses for six or seven hours each day in preparation for the 10 minutes he spends performing under the lights. He continues practicing until just before going onstage.

“Juggling requires such a precise touch that you can lose the right feel within minutes,” he explained. “A lot of different conditions can interfere. Humidity makes completing my routine extremely challenging. Wind matters, too—even a small air current can shift a ring by an inch when you’re preparing to catch it, and that’s enough to make you miss.”

During his routine, however, he almost never does.

Although his livelihood depends on focus and coordination for 350 performances each year, Gatto says his most humiliating mishap did not involve rings, clubs or balls. Instead, acting is what causes him trouble.

“I’ve fallen while playing the show’s delivery-man character,” he said. “Actually, it has happened several times. I prefer to believe it’s because I commit myself completely to the roles I’m playing.”

Amid such remarkable skill and exactness, it is reassuring to learn that one of the world’s finest jugglers—perhaps the very best—can also be clumsy.

# Anthony Gatto made juggling look easy. That was the hard part.

**Under the lights of Cirque du Soleil’s “Kooza,” the record-setting performer turned split-second precision into something close to magic.**

Anthony Gatto walked into the spotlight carrying the tools of his trade: balls, rings and clubs.

Then gravity seemed to loosen its grip.

Objects rose above him in clean, symmetrical arcs. Clubs spun into his hands with the regularity of clockwork. Rings flashed beneath the big top as the music accelerated and the audience leaned forward, waiting for the pattern to collapse.

It rarely did.

As a featured performer in Cirque du Soleil’s touring production “Kooza,” Gatto brought one of juggling’s most formidable résumés to a show built around traditional circus skills. His act was not disguised as illusion. There were no trapdoors or camera tricks — only repetition, timing and a lifetime of training compressed into a few breathless minutes.

Gatto began juggling as a small child, coached by his father, Nick. By the time most children were learning to tie their shoes, he was already developing the coordination that would carry him onto stages around the world.

He became a professional while still young and went on to dominate the technical side of the art. Over the years, Gatto set multiple juggling records with balls, rings and clubs, combining unusually high numbers of objects with an ability to keep them aloft for sustained periods. In 2000, he received the Golden Clown at the International Circus Festival of Monte-Carlo, one of the circus world’s highest honors.

Yet statistics alone do not explain his appeal.

Juggling at Gatto’s level is an exercise in managing failure. A throw can drift by a fraction of an inch. A club can rotate slightly too fast. A hand can close a moment too late. The audience sees a flowing pattern; the juggler sees hundreds of tiny corrections.

That tension made his “Kooza” performance especially effective. The production, which premiered in 2007, marked a return to Cirque du Soleil’s circus roots, emphasizing acrobatics, clowning and physical risk. Among its towering wheels, contortionists and high-wire performers, Gatto often appeared alone, relying on little more than his hands and the expectation that, eventually, something had to fall.

His calm suggested otherwise.

As the number of objects increased, the act’s mood shifted. What began as playful became improbable. The patterns climbed higher and moved faster until individual throws blurred into a single moving shape.

The difficulty was obvious, but the labor behind it remained invisible. That was part of Gatto’s skill: He made years of disciplined practice look spontaneous.

For elite jugglers, endurance is as important as dexterity. Training places repeated stress on the shoulders, elbows and wrists, while the mind must stay fixed on rhythm and trajectory. A world-record attempt or major stage performance can be undone by one lapse in concentration.

Gatto built his career by minimizing those lapses. Fellow jugglers regarded him not merely as an entertainer but as a benchmark — the performer whose videos were studied frame by frame and whose records helped define what was technically possible.

After decades in the ring, Gatto eventually stepped away from professional juggling. His departure surprised admirers accustomed to seeing him at the top of the field, but it also underscored the demanding reality behind the polished stage persona. Even extraordinary physical careers have limits, and life beyond the spotlight can offer a different kind of satisfaction.

What remains is the image of Gatto beneath the “Kooza” lights, looking upward as clubs and rings crossed above his head.

For the audience, the moment felt precarious.

For Gatto, it was the product of a lifetime: throw, turn, catch — and repeat until the impossible looked routine.

## Backstage at Cirque du Soleil, Where Flying Objects Are All in a Day’s Work

Backstage at Cirque du Soleil, the air smells faintly of makeup, sweat and imminent catastrophe.

Performers stretch in improbable directions. Technicians check ropes and rigging. Costumes glitter from crowded racks. Then, in a relatively bare patch of floor, Anthony Gatto begins throwing things.

First come the balls, rising in clean, even arcs. Then rings flash above his head. Finally, clubs tumble end over end, each one apparently assigned its own invisible lane through the air. Gatto stands at the center, quiet and economical, while the space above him turns into controlled weather.

Watching him practice is less like seeing a circus trick than peering inside a precision instrument. His hands make tiny corrections. His eyes stay fixed near the top of the pattern. Nothing seems hurried, even when the number of objects becomes difficult to count.

This serenity was not acquired overnight—although Gatto started early enough to make it seem that way.

Born into a circus family, he began learning to juggle at about 4 under the close supervision of his father, Nick Gatto, a former performer. The elder Gatto approached juggling as both craft and discipline. He made equipment for his son, studied technique and organized training so that difficult skills were built one small step at a time.

By 5, Anthony was appearing in shows. At an age when most children were still mastering shoelaces, he was mastering cascade patterns and public performance. His childhood included long, repetitive practice sessions: throws, catches, corrections, then the same sequence again. The goal was not simply to keep objects aloft but to make every throw nearly identical.

That training is still visible in his daily routine. Before a performance, Gatto warms up gradually rather than charging straight into the most dangerous combinations. He works through simpler patterns, checks the speed and height of his throws, and adjusts to the room. Ceiling height, lighting, temperature and even a stray draft can matter when several clubs are rotating inches apart.

The routine is repetition-heavy by design. A Cirque audience may see only a few polished minutes, but those minutes rest on years of drills and daily maintenance. Gatto practices transitions as carefully as the headline feats: picking up the next prop, changing rhythm, moving across the stage and recovering without breaking character.

The results made him one of the most celebrated technical jugglers of his generation. He established a formidable collection of records, including marks for keeping seven balls in the air for more than 10 minutes, eight balls for more than a minute and nine balls for roughly 54 seconds. He also set major records with clubs, including six- and seven-club runs. Some records have since been challenged or surpassed, but together they helped define the outer limits of juggling during his career.

Records, however, can give the wrong impression. They suggest a smooth upward march: more objects, longer times, louder applause. Practice tells the less glamorous truth.

Things hit each other.

A club clips another club and shoots sideways. A ball lands on a foot and rolls under equipment. A ring catches the light at the wrong angle, forcing an emergency grab. Occasionally a prop heads toward a musician, a curtain or an innocent backstage observer who suddenly discovers excellent reflexes.

Gatto treats such mishaps without drama. He retrieves the runaway object, resets his stance and begins again. A dropped club is not a tragedy; it is information.

Onstage, he can turn the occasional error into comedy, acknowledging it with a look or a shrug before rebuilding the pattern. That is part of the circus skill, too. The audience may admire perfection, but it often loves recovery even more.

Backstage, the astonishing thing is not that Gatto never drops. It is how quickly failure disappears into the routine. One moment, clubs clatter across the floor. The next, seven objects are circling above him again, orderly as planets.

Around him, Cirque du Soleil continues its busy preparations—acrobats warming up, dressers hurrying past, stagehands speaking into headsets. Gatto keeps throwing.

For a few minutes, gravity appears to have been invited to the rehearsal merely as a courtesy.

# Meet Anthony Gatto, the juggling legend who never drops the ball

**By CNN**

Anthony Gatto did not exactly stumble into juggling. He began training at age 3—an age when most children are still mastering spoons, shoelaces and the fine art of staying upright.

That early start paid off. Gatto became one of the world’s most celebrated jugglers, dazzling audiences with routines involving balls, rings and clubs traveling through the air at seemingly impossible speeds.

His commitment was every bit as remarkable as his performances. Gatto has practiced six to seven hours a day, turning split-second timing and relentless repetition into a career at the top of his craft.

He also holds 11 world records, cementing his reputation as an elite performer with an almost superhuman ability to keep objects aloft.

And then there is the celebrity footnote: Gatto once beat actor Patrick Dempsey—yes, *that* Patrick Dempsey—in a juggling competition. Long before becoming known to television audiences as “McDreamy,” Dempsey was an accomplished juggler. Against Gatto, however, even his well-honed skills were not enough.

For Gatto, juggling has always been more than a novelty act. It is a discipline built on precision, stamina and thousands upon thousands of catches.

Still, his career offers one reassuring lesson for the rest of us: If you ever feel as though you have too many balls in the air, be thankful there are not 11 world records riding on them.

### The Juggler Who Never Misses—Except When He Walks

Backstage at Cirque du Soleil’s *Kooza*, Anthony Gatto stood amid the ordinary clutter of an extraordinary job: clubs arranged by size, rings stacked flat, balls waiting in neat rows. Beyond the curtain, the production’s madcap world was already in motion—acrobats warming up, musicians tuning, stagehands checking cues.

Gatto’s preparations were quieter. He rolled his shoulders, tested the weight of a prop and rehearsed small pieces of movement with the economy of someone who had repeated them tens of thousands of times.

Then he stepped into the light.

Onstage, Gatto appeared to operate under a private set of physical laws. Balls rose in clean, interlocking arcs. Rings sliced through the air. Clubs rotated with such consistency that their handles seemed destined for his hands. He changed patterns without disturbing their rhythm, adding objects and difficulty until the audience’s applause took on a disbelieving edge.

Gatto, widely regarded as one of the finest technical jugglers of his generation, built his reputation on numbers that sound almost implausible: nine balls, seven clubs, 11 rings. Yet his *Kooza* act was more than a demonstration of quantity. Its force came from precision—the exact height of a throw, the measured fraction of a second between catches, the composure required to make extreme difficulty look inevitable.

That control was especially striking inside *Kooza*, a show that returns Cirque du Soleil to the imagery of the traditional circus while surrounding its acts with clowns, extravagant costumes and a storybook sense of danger. Gatto’s juggling fit naturally into that world, but it also interrupted it. For several minutes, chaos narrowed into geometry.

Backstage, however, the illusion of perfect coordination gave way to a more human confession: Gatto acknowledged that while acting in the production, he sometimes tripped.

The admission sounded almost comic coming from a man capable of tracking multiple objects moving above, below and around him. But it revealed the difference between the skills audiences tend to group together under the label of “coordination.” Juggling was Gatto’s native language, developed through relentless practice from childhood. Acting required another kind of awareness—costume, character, timing, marks on the floor and the movements of other performers.

In the juggling act, every motion had a purpose. In a theatrical scene, he sometimes had to appear spontaneous while obeying an invisible map.

That contrast also exposed the labor beneath his apparent effortlessness. Gatto’s precision was not a magical, all-purpose gift. It was highly specialized mastery, built one throw and one correction at a time. He knew how a club should leave his hand, how many rotations it needed and where it would descend. Walking in character across a crowded stage could be less predictable.

From the audience, his act seemed suspended between risk and certainty. A single bad throw could disturb the whole pattern, yet Gatto rarely allowed spectators to see the calculations. His face remained calm. His catches landed softly. The objects appeared less tossed than placed in the air.

Backstage, the props eventually returned to their cases. The rings stopped flashing; the clubs became inert pieces of wood and tape. Gatto, no longer the fixed point at the center of a storm, moved again through the practical world of curtains, cables and costume changes—a world in which even a legendary juggler could catch his foot.

That may have been the most revealing trick of all. Onstage, Anthony Gatto made the impossible look natural. Offstage, he admitted that the simplest movement could still surprise him.
